explain.say: Picture a man rowing across freezing grey water. His lord is dead, his friends are buried, and there is no hall left to go home to. That is The Wanderer, copied into the Exeter Book around 970. The panels tell his story.

explain.say: Look at panels three and four. He falls asleep and dreams he is back in the hall, kneeling before his lord. Then he wakes to waves, seabirds bathing and snow falling. The poem lives in that gap between memory and now. Have you ever woken from a happy dream to a sad morning?

explain.say: The Seafarer is its companion poem. On the left, the Wanderer: exile is forced on him. On the right, the Seafarer: he chooses the cold sea, hungry and alone, because worldly glory fades. Ezra Pound made a famous version in 1911. Which speaker would you rather be?

explain.say: Both poems end by turning to patience and heavenly comfort. Older critics thought monks bolted those endings on; most now read them as part of the design. Here are the features to spot. Beautiful work. Challenge: write three lines of your own asking where something has gone.

faq.q: What is an Old English elegy?
faq.a: A short, sombre poem about loss, exile and the passing of earthly things, usually ending in some kind of consolation. The Wanderer, The Seafarer and The Ruin are famous examples.

faq.q: What is the ubi sunt motif?
faq.a: From the Latin for where are they? It is a lament that asks where the people, joys and splendours of the past have gone, as the Wanderer does looking at ruined walls.
A large collection of Old English poetry, copied around 970 and given to Exeter Cathedral by Bishop Leofric. It holds The Wanderer, The Seafarer and nearly a hundred riddles.
asks: Where are The Wanderer and The Seafarer found?

faq.q: How is The Seafarer different from The Wanderer?
faq.a: The Wanderer is forced into exile and mourns his lord. The Seafarer seems to choose the hardship of the sea, and moves from describing it to reflecting that earthly glory fades.
Earlier scholars thought they were added later. Most critics now see them as integral: the poems move from earthly loss to a hope that lasts beyond the world.
asks: Were the religious endings added later?
